docs.summary: Caps and conversions applied to a decode. The limits exist because image headers are attacker controlled: a four byte width field can claim two billion pixels. Every decoder checks the declared geometry against these before allocating anything, so a malicious file fails with [`LimitExceeded`](#api~Prowl.Aperture.ApertureError~LimitExceeded) instead of exhausting the process.
Shared instance with the default limits. Treat as immutable.
Convert the decoded pixels to this layout. Null keeps whatever the decoder produces naturally, reported by [`PreferredPixelFormat`](#api~Prowl.Aperture.ImageInfo~PreferredPixelFormat).
Largest accepted width in pixels.
Largest accepted height in pixels.

Largest accepted pixel count for a single frame. Bounds the aspect ratio abuse that slips past [`MaxWidth`](#api~Prowl.Aperture.DecodeOptions~MaxWidth) and [`MaxHeight`](#api~Prowl.Aperture.DecodeOptions~MaxHeight) individually.
Largest total buffer a single decode may allocate for pixel data.
Largest number of frames read from an animation or a multi-image container.
Decode every frame of an animated or multi-image file. When false only the primary image is decoded, which is what a texture loader normally wants.
Decode the mipmap chain of container formats that store one, currently DDS and KTX style textures. When false only the largest level is read.

Rotate and flip decoded pixels to match the Exif orientation tag. Off by default, because a quarter turn trades the width for the height and would put a decode at odds with [`Identify`](#api~Prowl.Aperture.Image~Identify). The tag is on [`Orientation`](#api~Prowl.Aperture.ImageInfo~Orientation) either way.

Return the rows that were recovered when a stream ends early, instead of failing with [`UnexpectedEndOfData`](#api~Prowl.Aperture.ApertureError~UnexpectedEndOfData). Useful for showing a partial download; a build pipeline usually wants the failure.
Reject a file whose embedded checksums do not match. When false a bad CRC is ignored as long as the data still decodes, which is how most viewers behave.
Keep Exif, XMP and ICC blocks on the decoded [`Image`](#api~Prowl.Aperture.Image).

Pads every row out to a multiple of this many bytes. One packs the rows with no gap; setting the row pitch a graphics API reported makes the decoder write straight into that layout rather than the caller re-striding afterwards.
Writes the bottom row of the image first, which is the order a lower left texture origin wants. It costs nothing here, where flipping afterwards is a second pass over the image.

Rent pixel memory from the shared array pool rather than allocating it. This is what makes repeated loads cheap, and it is why [`Image`](#api~Prowl.Aperture.Image) is disposable. Turn it off when the pixel buffer has to outlive the image it came from.
Creates a copy so a caller can tweak one knob without mutating a shared instance.
